co_cortez_hawkins_preserve.blurb: A small sandstone escarpment on the edge of Cortez, running about half a mile along the north side of McElmo Creek. The rim is low, roughly 6 to 30 feet, and the problems on it include overhangs, cracks, arêtes and patinated slabs. Most lines fall between V0 and V4 with a few harder ones, which makes it a good place for easy-to-moderate circuits and technique work. Classics include The Van, Skinny Dihedral and Hawkins Black-on-White. The climbing is split into east, central and west sections, and the east side is the most developed. It is a quiet spot and an easy stop on the way to Mesa Verde.
co_cortez_hawkins_preserve.parking_note: Park in the lot off Oak Street in southern Cortez; the trail to the rim leaves from there.
co_cortez_hawkins_preserve.approach: Take the first trail heading south, about half a mile over pitted sandstone bedrock. Cairns mark the way, and a white sign shows where to drop down to the boulders.

co_rigid_designator_amphitheatre.blurb: Vail's best-known ice amphitheatre, a north-facing wall of short ice and mixed lines just above town. Most climbs are one or two pitches, from slabby sheets and free-hanging pillars to steep drytooling, and most have anchors at the top so lines can be top-roped. The ice is mostly WI5 and WI6, and the mixed lines run from moderate up to M11. Classics include Rigid Designator, The Fang, Octopussy, Seventh Tentacle and Red Bull and Vodka. It is popular and easy to see from the interstate, so expect company. Because it faces north it stays cold, so dress warmly, and the hardest part of the day can be finding a place to leave the car.
co_rigid_designator_amphitheatre.parking_note: Park in a legal spot in Vail, such as the Pumphouse lot, and walk east along the frontage road to Aspen Lane.
co_rigid_designator_amphitheatre.approach: From the cul-de-sac at the end of Aspen Court, cross the footbridge over the creek and turn left onto the climber's trail. It crosses the golf course, then gains about 550 feet to the base of Rigid Designator and The Fang.

co_amphitheater_the.blurb: A compact crag in Gregory Canyon at the north end of the Flatirons, just west of Boulder. The climbs are short and mostly traditional, with a few top-ropes, a couple of boulder problems and a lone sport line. Grades run from beginner scrambles and easy leads through the 5.9 to 5.10 range, with a few 5.11s and 5.12s such as P.S. I'm Blonde. Parking near the trailhead is popular and limited, so arrive early or be ready to walk from farther away. Poison ivy is thick in the canyon in season, and bears and mountain lions live in the area.
co_amphitheater_the.parking_note: Most climbers use the Gregory Canyon trailhead off Baseline Road; the lot fills quickly, with overflow on nearby streets or at Chautauqua, about 0.6 miles away.

co_piano_ridge.blurb: A short west-facing ridge of easy-to-moderate boulders on the Horsetooth side of Fort Collins, a few steps from the car. The problems are cracks, roofs, slabs, arêtes and slopers, and most go at V0 to V3, with a handful of V4s, one V5 and one outlier much harder. It is a handy spot for a quick session, with plenty of traverses and short up-lines for warming up. Continental Shelf, Piano Traverse and Sloper Traverse (aka Baby Grand) are the ones to try first. Bring pads, and expect afternoon sun on the rock since the ridge faces west.
co_piano_ridge.parking_note: Use the lot on the east side of Centennial Drive, roughly half a mile north of County Road 38E.
co_piano_ridge.approach: A signed trail begins in the middle of the lot and runs about 400 feet east to the boulders.

co_helen_s_dome.blurb: A big granite dome in the South Platte country, west of Cheesman Reservoir. The climbing is mostly face work on friction slabs, where feldspar crystals give the rock some texture, with a few pure crack lines and short cracks on many faces. Bolts protect the faces, while the cracks take a light rack of small to medium gear. Grades cluster around 5.9 and 5.10, with some easier and a few 5.11s. Sticks 'n' Stones, Beam Me Up, Scotty and Helen Wheels are among the favorites. The routes face west, so the sun arrives mid-morning and stays into the evening. Come down by rappel with double ropes or the walk-off; the trail is slippery when wet.
co_helen_s_dome.parking_note: Follow the forest road from the Deckers area toward Goose Creek and Molly Gulch; a pullout about 7.7 miles from the pavement serves the trail to the dome.
co_helen_s_dome.approach: Cross the creek on a log, follow the path up through a boulder field, then scramble a short crack to the shelf at the base of the routes.

_expect.name: Cactus Cliff Far Left (left of Muscle Beach)

co_a_cactus_cliff_far_left_left_of_muscl.blurb: The far left end of Cactus Cliff, one of the tallest and best-rounded sport walls at Shelf Road near Cañon City. The limestone here is sustained and crimpy, and almost every line is bolted, with a few trad routes mixed in. Most routes are 5.10 to 5.12, with a scattering of easier and harder ones, so it suits strong intermediates and up. Crynoid Corner is an easy 5.7 warm-up, while Illegal Smile (5.11b) and Hair Trigger are better known for the harder crowd. The cliff faces south, which makes it a popular winter choice and a hot place in summer.
co_a_cactus_cliff_far_left_left_of_muscl.parking_note: Park in the lot at The Bank and walk in from there.
co_a_cactus_cliff_far_left_left_of_muscl.approach: From the lot, follow the road a short way, then take the trail on the right down into the canyon. Cross the bottom and climb to the maintained trail that runs along the base of the cliff.

co_anti_phil_wall.blurb: One of the larger sport zones in Rifle Mountain Park, a tall, steep limestone wall that lies across the stream from the picnic area. The routes here are long and sustained rather than pulling through big caves like those elsewhere in the canyon. The rock varies from pale to grey-blue and is generally solid. This is a hard-climber's wall: almost everything is 5.11 or harder, with most of it at 5.12 and 5.13. Easy Skankin', I Am Not A Philistine, Phil of All Evil and The Anti-Phil are among the best known. Many route names are puns on the name Phil.
co_anti_phil_wall.parking_note: Use the picnic area a few hundred yards down the canyon from Ruckman Cave.
co_anti_phil_wall.approach: Cross the stream on the plank bridge, where a tree helps, and pick up the trail on the far side. Walk a short way downstream; this is the first wall you reach.

co_streaked_wall.blurb: The largest wall in the Falls Walls group above Telluride, marked by big dark streaks. The rock is pocketed conglomerate with a bit of a limestone feel, and nearly every route is bolted sport. It is the place to come for 5.11 and 5.12 climbing, with a few 5.10s and a good handful of 5.13s. Gray Matter, The Nomad, Fool's Gold, Watermusic and Hydropower are the ones people mention most. The walls get sun only until around midday, and the hike in involves a creek crossing, so allow time and expect to get your feet wet at high water.
co_streaked_wall.approach: The Falls Walls share one trail from the dirt road east of town; cross the creek and climb to the walls. A faint path breaks off to the left, below the lingering snowfield, to reach Streaked Wall.

co_black_hole_the.blurb: The best-known cave and roof zone among the Morrison boulders, on the hogback just outside Denver. The rock is hard sandstone, and the problems are steep, powerful and often greasy, with slopers, sharp crimps and plenty of eliminates and linkups. This is a hard-climber's venue: most problems are V5 and up, with just a few easier lines such as Breashears' Crack. Helicopter, Pressure Sensitive and Extra Otis are well-known tests. Summer heat makes the slick holds miserable, so cooler months suit it best.
